title: Stage 1: Reading lines
summary: Read everything from standard input, skip the lines that are not data, and split the rest into columns.

steps.title: What you are building
body: Every company has a spreadsheet of expenses that someone exports as text and then needs summarised. Over this project you will build the tool that does it: a **command-line program** that reads raw expense lines, throws out the broken ones with a clear reason, and prints a report.
The input is one expense per line, with four values separated by commas:

By the last stage your program turns a messy file of these into a report with totals per category and per month, a list of expenses that break company policy, and a list of the lines it could not read.
Your code carries forward: each step starts from what you finished in the step before.
First the plumbing. Read every line, skip the ones that are not data, and split the rest into columns. For the input above your program will print:

steps.prompt: The tool reads from **standard input** instead of opening a file by name. In a terminal you would run it as `expenses < march.csv`. What is the main advantage?
options: The same program works with a file, with another program's output, or with text the tests feed it
Standard input is faster than reading a file
The program does not need a loop to read standard input
Standard input removes badly formed lines automatically
steps.explain: The program does not care where the text comes from. That is what makes small command-line tools easy to combine, and easy to test: the tests here simply hand your program some lines and read what it prints.

steps.title: Reading until the input ends
body: `Console.ReadLine()` returns the next line of input. When there is nothing left it returns **`null`**. That is the only signal you get, so the loop that reads a whole input looks like this:
Read the condition from the inside out: read a line, store it in `line`, then check that what was stored is not `null`. The type is `string?` because it really can be `null`.
> **Tip:** An empty line is not the end of the input. It comes back as the empty string `""`, and the loop keeps going.

steps.prompt: The input has three lines: `red`, then an empty line, then `blue`. What does this print?
steps.explain: The empty line is a line like any other: `ReadLine` returns `""` for it, which is not `null`. Only the end of the input returns `null`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a program that stores every line of input in a list and then prints how many there were.
steps.explain: Declare what the loop needs, loop until `ReadLine` returns `null`, and only then report. The two declarations can go in either order.

steps.title: Count the lines
prompt: Start the tool. Read **every** line of standard input until it ends, and keep the lines in a `List<string>`.
Blank lines are noise: exports often end with a few. Do not keep a line that is empty or only spaces.
Then print how many lines you kept, in exactly this form:
With no input at all, print `Lines: 0`.
starter: // Read every line of standard input, keep the ones that are not blank,
// then print how many you kept.
hints: Use the loop from the card: `while ((line = Console.ReadLine()) is not null)`.
`string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(line)` is `true` for an empty line and for one that is only spaces. `continue;` jumps to the next turn of the loop.
Inside the loop: `if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(line)) continue;` then `lines.Add(line);`. After the loop: `Console.WriteLine($"Lines: {lines.Count}");`

steps.title: From lines to columns
body: A line such as `2026-03-04,Travel,45.50,Taxi to airport` is still one string. `Split` cuts it at a separator and gives you an array of the pieces:
`string.Join` goes the other way. It glues the pieces back together with whatever you put between them, which is handy for showing what you parsed:
The first line of an export is usually a **header** naming the columns. It is not an expense, so the program must skip it. Ours always starts with `date,`:

steps.prompt: Someone left the amount out. What does this print?
steps.explain: Two commas in a row still separate two columns. The one between them is an empty string, so there are 4 parts and the third has length 0. `Split` never skips a column unless you ask it to.

steps.prompt: Complete the loop so that it skips blank lines and stores the columns of every other line.
steps.explain: `continue` skips to the next line of input. `break` would stop reading at the first blank line and silently lose everything after it.

steps.title: Split into rows
prompt: Turn the lines into **rows**. Change the program so that it:
- also skips the header line (any line that starts with `date,`),
- splits every other line on commas and keeps the pieces in a `List<string[]>`.
Then print each row with its columns joined by ` | ` (space, bar, space), followed by the number of rows. For this input:
The header is optional. With no rows, print only `Rows: 0`.

tests.name: header, two rows and blank lines

hints: The list now holds arrays: `var rows = new List<string[]>();` and `rows.Add(line.Split(','));`.
Add a second skip under the blank-line check: `if (line.StartsWith("date,")) continue;`
After the loop: `foreach (var row in rows) Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" | ", row));` then `Console.WriteLine($"Rows: {rows.Count}");`
